newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan official welcomes dollar rise.
newsitem.headline: Japan official welcomes dollar rise.

text.p: An influential Japanese finance ministry official said on Thursday that he welcomed currency developments since April 1995 when the dollar started rebounding from its record low against the yen.
Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of the ministry's International Finance Bureau, also told reporters that Japan's policy on foreign exchange has not changed.
Currency markets have been affected in the past by comments by Sakakibara, who is dubbed "Mr. Yen" because of his influence over dollar-yen exchange rates.

And the markets have grown extra nervous about what Sakakibara has to say about Japan's currency policies since last week when an article in a Japanese financial paper quoted him as saying the dollar's correction of last year's sharp slide against the yen was about to finish.
That report pushed down the dollar sharply from about 115 yen. It briefly edged up after Sakakibara's latest comments and was hovering around 111.60 yen in late Tokyo trade.
The dollar has rebounded since April 1995 when it hit a record low of 79.75 yen.

"The foreign exchange policy of Japan's Ministry of Finance has not changed. We welcome the developments that have taken place in foreign exchange markets since April 1995," Sakakibara told reporters.
But one currency dealer said the comments were in line with a foreign exchange policy sought by and agreed with G7 nations and were not enough to spur fresh buying of the dollar against the yen.

"The comments were nothing extraordinary. Market participants can't buy the dollar on the comments as U.S. funds appear to be interested in selling the dollar when the greenback rises," said Yoshitaka Niwa, a manager at ING Bank in Tokyo.
Senior Japanese government officials have recently said the dollar was still in the process of an orderly reversal.
"Cooperation among the Group of Seven industrialised nations on currencies remains unchanged," Sakakibara said.
Japan has been in favour of the yen's decline against the dollar since last year as the strong yen had hurt Japanese exporters, slowing the country's economic recovery.
A strong yen makes Japanese products more expensive abroad, thus cutting into the competitive edge of Japanese exporters.
